High Energy Efficiency Plasma Conversion of CO2at Atmospheric Pressure Using a Direct-Coupled Microwave Plasma System
top_cited_works.abstract: Energy and conversion efficiencies of the carbon dioxide (CO2) dissociation process at atmospheric-pressure conditions are investigated using a direct-coupled continuous microwave plasma system (MPS). Gas chromatography and mass spectrometer measurements were performed on the gas mixture postplasma treatment, over a range of specific energy inputs (SEIs) (0.06–0.6 eV mol$^{-1})$, in order to determine species mass fractions of CO2, carbon monoxide, and oxygen. In this region of SEI, energy efficiency is maximized at the cost of conversion efficiency. The corresponding maximum observed quantities for conversion efficiency and energy conversion efficiency (ECE) occurred at conditions close to the end of the test range and are, respectively, 9% and 0.0048 L min$^{-1}\text{W}^{-1}$. The maximum throughput of CO2converted was 0.59 L min$^{-1}$, at an SEI of 0.1 eV mol$^{-1}$and an ECE of 0.004 L min$^{-1}\text{W}^{-1}$. Optical emission spectroscopy was used to approximate the rotational and vibrational temperatures of the plasma system to be in the range of 7000–8000 K. recent_works.title: Total Cost of Ownership Reduction Using Passive Pre-Chamber Ignition in Natural Gas Engines
recent_works.venue: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
recent_works.abstract: Spark plug durability is a factor affecting the total cost of ownership (TCO) of spark-ignited natural gas engines, with some heavy-duty platforms requiring plug replacement after only 750 hours of operation. The high ignition energy demand under lean or diluted conditions accelerates electrode wear, shortening plug life and increasing maintenance frequency. This work evaluates passive pre-chamber (PC) ignition operating at lowered spark energies as a strategy to reduce spark energy requirements and extend plug durability, thereby lowering TCO. Experiments were conducted on a medium-duty Cummins 6.7L ISB engine at 1600 RPM and 50% load under varying exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) dilution levels (0–40%). Two passive pre-chambers with 1.1 mm and 1.6 mm nozzle diameters were compared with conventional spark ignition (SI). SI was operated with a fixed coil dwell of 4 ms (~90 mJ), while the PC configuration was tested across 2–4 ms dwell times (~30–90 mJ). Cylinder pressure analysis revealed that PC ignition sustained stable combustion at significantly lower spark energies than SI, with improved combustion stability at ~30 mJ compared with SI at ~90 mJ. Machine Learning-Augmented Flame Front Detection in High-Speed Imaging: A Physics-Guided Framework
recent_works.abstract: High-speed combustion imaging provides critical insight into ignition, flame-kernel evolution, and turbulent flame propagation in advanced propulsion systems. However, extracting physically meaningful flame boundaries from such data remains challenging due to low signal-to-noise ratio, rapid luminosity variation, window fouling, and interference from shot noise and internal chemiluminescence gradients. Conventional image-processing workflows, typically based on thresholding, morphological operations, or classical gradient filters, require extensive manual tuning and often produce fragmented or non-physical flame contours that do not generalize across operating conditions. This work presents AGNI AI-Guided aNalysis for Image data. We currently evaluate the AGNI framework for flame-edge detection using high-speed OH∗ chemiluminescence images from a spark-ignited hydrogen-fueled heavy-duty optical engine. recent_works.title: Spatially resolved knock onset measurements and 0-D predictions in an optical heavy-duty natural gas engine
recent_works.abstract: Engine knock remains a major barrier to improving efficiency and expanding the use of natural gas (NG) in heavy-duty engines. This study combines optical diagnostics, in-cylinder pressure measurements, and detailed kinetic modeling to investigate knock-onset (KO) behavior under controlled mild-knock conditions. A modified heavy-duty diesel engine fueled with a well-characterized synthetic NG mixture was used to acquire cycle-resolved OH* chemiluminescence and pressure data, enabling both temporal and spatial identification of KO across bowl, squish, and crevice regions. The measured pressure trace was then imposed on an adiabatic zero-dimensional (0-D) reactor model to evaluate the KO-prediction capability of four chemical-kinetic mechanisms. Modern mechanisms (Miller, AramcoMech 2.0, CSU141) reproduced KO timing to within 2 °CA ( ≈ ± 0.3 ms) for all KO locations, while the legacy GRI-Mech 3.0 showed significantly larger deviations. Notably, prediction accuracy exhibited no dependence on the spatial origin of KO, despite substantial cycle-to-cycle variability.
